source.title: Cross-Lingual Transfer of Evil Vectors Is Directionally Asymmetric

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies cross-lingual transfer of evil-persona vectors, not the refusal direction or refusal behavior specified by the claim versions. It cites the original refusal-direction paper but does not test or use that finding.
record.gate_note: The paper uses contrastive mean-difference vectors for evil versus unevil responses and measures evil-expression scores, MMLU, and vector geometry. These results concern evil-persona steering rather than refusal, so they are recorded as findings about a related construct under fits_no_version. The reference to the original refusal-direction study and the related-work mention of cross-lingual refusal representations are citations, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study extracts and adds mean-difference 'evil persona' vectors and scores evil expression with an LLM judge. It never measures refusal rates, ablates a refusal direction, or edits weights. The original refusal-direction paper (arXiv:2406.11717) is cited only as related work on linear representations. Wang et al. 2026 on cross-lingual refusal is likewise only cited. The cross-lingual results concern a different construct (an evil trait, not refusal), so they belong under fits_no_version and give no V6 evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. One addition: the authors infer that a shared evil direction exists and is present in low-resource languages, but is hard to recover from low-resource data. They argue a single high-resource vector can be reused without per-language data collection.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a contrastive mean-difference activation vector and activation addition, but for evil versus unevil responses rather than harmful versus harmless instructions for refusal; it adds the vector at a selected layer rather than ablating a refusal direction across layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome differs by extraction-language resource level and transfer direction: high-resource-to-low-resource steering is effective, whereas low-resource-to-high-resource transfer offers no improvement. Low-resource self-steering is markedly weaker.

fits_no_version.finding: Evil vectors from English/Spanish steer Swahili/Telugu inputs to high Evil Expression Score (EES). Swahili/Telugu vectors are weak even on their own language and give no improvement on English/Spanish inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Evil-persona mean-difference vectors transfer asymmetrically across languages, from high-resource to low-resource but not the reverse.

fits_no_version.finding: With high-resource evil vectors at α=3, MMLU on low-resource languages stays near the unsteered baseline in all four models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-resource evil-vector steering largely preserves MMLU on low-resource inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at layer ℓ*, the EN–ES cosine is 0.94. Swahili is -0.13/-0.12 against EN/ES and Telugu is 0.28/0.30.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High-resource-language evil vectors share a direction that low-resource extraction recovers poorly.

record.problems: Evil-expression scores rely on LLM judges, despite using two judge models. The evaluation covers only two high-resource and two low-resource languages. Main steering and MMLU results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text, and the geometric analysis is reported for Qwen2.5-7B.

untested.parts: All of it: no refusal direction, no ablation, no refusal induction, no refusal rates.
All of it: no weight-edit or abliteration.
All of it: no jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training.
All of it: no comparison of single versus multiple refusal directions.
All of it: no separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Cross-lingual transfer of a refusal direction is not tested; only evil-persona vectors are. Model-variant and base-to-instruct transfer are also untested.
All of it: training is not varied.
All of it: no reasoning models.

record.verdict_notes: The evil-vector recipe (mean difference plus activation addition) resembles the refusal-direction method, but its target is an evil trait scored by an LLM judge. The judge template has a REFUSAL output option, but no refusal rates are reported. The claim that adding the evil vector 'forces adversarial compliance' is cited from Feng et al. 2026, not measured here. No verdicts are given because no row bears on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether a refusal direction mediates refusal, whether ablating it removes refusal, whether adding it induces harmless-request refusals, or the effect on general abilities.
No weight-edit or abliteration procedure is tested.
The study does not test jailbreak suppression of the refusal direction or robustness training against its ablation.
The study does not compare single-direction refusal accounts with affine, cone, or multi-direction accounts.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
The study tests cross-language transfer of evil-persona vectors, not transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
The study does not vary refusal training or test how training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.
No reasoning models or reasoning-before-answering condition are tested.

rows.operation_detail: Counts high-quality positive evil responses retained for vector extraction after judge filtering.

conditions.value: English and Spanish versus Swahili and Telugu
1,000 raw positive responses per model and language

rows.measure: Number/proportion of positive samples retained for extraction
rows.value: Figure only; text states that Swahili and Telugu yield far fewer high-quality positive samples than English and Spanish.
rows.note: Reported as a cross-model pattern; no per-model counts are stated in the text. This measures evil-vector extraction quality, not refusal.
rows.check: This is an extraction-pipeline selection value: the count of judge-filtered positive samples used to build the vector. It is not a steering outcome. The 'partial' state has no reference version and should be dropped or treated as descriptive.
